By killing himself, does such a person merely anticipate the killing that would otherwise be done by the enemy?

Or is it the entire condition of civil war—the self-destruction, the suicide of the makros anthrōpos, the great collective human being—that, although it neither justifies nor excuses the suicide of the individual participant, nevertheless absorbs it through the specific force of the situation?
If my name appears on a proscription list, why should I not be permitted to kill myself?

I kill myself only so that I do not give the enemy the triumph of murdering me. It is not I who take my life. The enemy takes it from me. I determine only the modus moriendi: the manner of my death. I take back my human dignity, which the enemy intended to take from me. And I deprive my enemy of the pleasure of giving me an undignified death. That is what distinguishes this kind of suicide in an acute civil war. It is the final expression of the human being’s free power of self-determination. It does not interfere with God’s sovereign power. It interferes with the murderous claims made by my human enemies.
Inside the space of a war that has no recognized form, different standards apply from those that apply elsewhere.

This is the absolute state of exception experienced by an individual pushed into the most extreme defenselessness: the outlaw who refuses to be stripped of his human dignity even when he is treated like an animal or like vermin.

The distinction between the personal and the real—between relations based on persons and relations based on things—is one of the primal principles of law and of all social life. These are the “two principles” whose opposition itself forms the primal principle.
Everyone who possesses property thinks in real terms. That means territorial terms for as long as the soil of the earth remains the most important res, the most important thing.
Everyone else thinks in personal terms: community as an association of human beings rather than an association built around things.
